<!-- Seven principles by which the fortress-repo skill is written as the curator would write it, each with its reason and a pair of texts from the skill's history, the one he marked and the one he accepted, for the writer of its parts. -->

# Writing the skills

The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.

## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else

A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."

## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them

A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."

## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest

Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"

## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work

A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."

Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.

## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name

A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."

## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace

The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."

Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.

## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read

A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.
- Marked: "`explorations/modernization-plan.md` gives the versions and the classfile level."
- Accepted: "Before you change the version of a tool, read its step in the modernization plan. [...] It prints 4 to 6 KB: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/modernization-plan.md#The ladder@TOOL'`."

80	
81	`tests-writing.md` says how a test names a refusal at load.
82	
83	Walk's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that varies from run to run. On one core, the order is fixed for a given library, but a library edit can change it. Do not pin or compare this order. The harness reads only that an `XXX` test fails.
84	
85	## Natives
86	
87	The library binds each of walk's natives by a declaration whose body is `builtinPrimitive("…")`. The string names one of these:
88	
89	- A glue class, as `com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X`, in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. A glue class takes the evaluator's boxed values, so the compiled path cannot use it. Most bindings name one.
90	- A helper: a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, as `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.<method>`. `glue/StaticNativeApp.java` calls it by reflection, with a method's `self` first. The compiled path calls it too (`compiler.md`, "Natives").
91	
92	Walk carries each declared type of a helper's binding in one Java type:
93	
94	- `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `Char` in `int`; `ZZ64` and `NN64` in `long`; `RR64` in `double`; `RR32` in `float`; `Boolean` in `boolean`;
95	- `String`, `FlatString` and `JavaString` in `String`; `ZZ` in `BigInteger`; `()` in `void`.
96	
97	Walk refuses a helper's binding at load in these cases. The message names the string, and contains the words below, which a `load_exception_contains` key can match:
98	
99	- The class or the method does not exist: 'not found' or 'names no static method of'.
100	- The result type, or a parameter type other than `self`'s, is not in the list above: 'no Java type carries the declared'.
101	- No method of that name, or more than one, has exactly the Java types of the list: 'has no overload that fits the declaration's types', or 'overloads that fit'.
102	
103	Walk does not check `self`. It passes `self` as the helper's first Java parameter, read as that parameter's Java type. So a binding in a method of a program's own type loads, and a `String` parameter receives the type's name (ledger row 847). Bind a helper in a method only if the helper's first Java parameter carries the type of `self`, as `int` for a method of `ZZ32`.
104	
105	A native declared over `String`, glue class or helper alike, receives the wrong text for a `CatString`: the name of the type, not its characters (ledger row 846). `||` builds a `CatString` when the joined string is longer than `maxLeafSize`, 32 characters by default. If a string that reaches such a native can come from `||`, pass it as `s.asFlatString` at the call of the native.
106	
107	An `import java` written in a `.fss` file is wired under walk but unfinished, and no test uses it. The compiled path's generated `import java` (`compiler.md`, "Natives") is not this one.
108	
109	A glue class raises a Fortress exception that a `catch` sees by throwing a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object. `Int.overflow()` in `Int.java` there makes one, and its callers throw it:
110	
111	    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
112	    return new FortressError(f);
113	
114	A helper runs on both paths, so it raises an exception as compiled code does: `throw Utility.makeFortressException("fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero")` (`compiler/runtimeValues/Utility.java`). The string names the compiler's prelude's class for the exception. Under walk, that class does not load, and `StaticNativeApp` raises the interpreter's library's object of the same name in its place. So raise from a helper only an exception that both libraries declare as an object, as `DivisionByZero` and `IntegerOverflow`. `ZZ32`'s `DIV` by zero raises `DivisionByZero` in this way. `tests-writing.md` says how a test names a refusal at load.

Walk's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that varies from run to run. On one core, the order is fixed for a given library, but a library edit can change it. Do not pin or compare this order. The harness reads only that an `XXX` test fails.

## Natives

The library binds each of walk's natives by a declaration whose body is `builtinPrimitive("…")`. The string names one of these:

- A glue class, as `com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X`, in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. A glue class takes the evaluator's boxed values, so the compiled path cannot use it. Most bindings name one.
- A helper: a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, as `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.<method>`. `glue/StaticNativeApp.java` calls it by reflection, with a method's `self` first. The compiled path calls it too (`compiler.md`, "Natives").

Walk carries each declared type of a helper's binding in one Java type:

- `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `Char` in `int`; `ZZ64` and `NN64` in `long`; `RR64` in `double`; `RR32` in `float`; `Boolean` in `boolean`;
- `String`, `FlatString` and `JavaString` in `String`; `ZZ` in `BigInteger`; `()` in `void`.

Walk refuses a helper's binding at load in these cases. The message names the string, and contains the words below, which a `load_exception_contains` key can match:

- The class or the method does not exist: 'not found' or 'names no static method of'.
- The result type, or a parameter type other than `self`'s, is not in the list above: 'no Java type carries the declared'.
- No method of that name, or more than one, has exactly the Java types of the list: 'has no overload that fits the declaration's types', or 'overloads that fit'.

Walk does not check `self`. It passes `self` as the helper's first Java parameter, read as that parameter's Java type. So a binding in a method of a program's own type loads, and a `String` parameter receives the type's name (ledger row 847). Bind a helper in a method only if the helper's first Java parameter carries the type of `self`, as `int` for a method of `ZZ32`.

A native declared over `String`, glue class or helper alike, receives the wrong text for a `CatString`: the name of the type, not its characters (ledger row 846). `||` builds a `CatString` when the joined string is longer than `maxLeafSize`, 32 characters by default. If a string that reaches such a native can come from `||`, pass it as `s.asFlatString` at the call of the native.

An `import java` written in a `.fss` file is wired under walk but unfinished, and no test uses it. The compiled path's generated `import java` (`compiler.md`, "Natives") is not this one.

A glue class raises a Fortress exception that a `catch` sees by throwing a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object. `Int.overflow()` in `Int.java` there makes one, and its callers throw it:

    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
    return new FortressError(f);

A helper runs on both paths, so it raises an exception as compiled code does: `throw Utility.makeFortressException("fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero")` (`compiler/runtimeValues/Utility.java`). The string names the compiler's prelude's class for the exception. Under walk, that class does not load, and `StaticNativeApp` raises the interpreter's library's object of the same name in its place. (* A function and a method whose where clause introduces a where-clause variable run compiled, the variable fixed by the call's arguments. *)
component XXXWhereVariableCallCompiled
export Executable

trait T
  f(): String
end
trait X[\nat n\] extends {T} end
trait Y[\nat m\] extends {T} end
object O extends {X[\1\]}
  f() = "O"
end
object P extends {Y[\1\]}
  f() = "P"
end
object Q
  m[\U\](u: U): String where [\nat n\]{U extends {X[\n\]}} = "m" || u.f()
end

g[\U, V\](u: U, v: V): String
    where [\nat n\]{U extends {X[\n\]}, V extends {Y[\n\]}} = u.f() || v.f()

run(): () = do
    println("REACHED")
    assert(g(O, P), "OP", "trait-parameters.tex, section \"Where Clauses\": a function's where clause introduces a where-clause variable")
    assert(Q.m(O), "mO", "trait-parameters.tex, section \"Where Clauses\": a method's where clause introduces a where-clause variable")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

(* A trait whose comprises clause lists a generic object at a where-clause type variable compiles and runs: its functional method, called through values of the trait's type, runs the trait's body on every listed instance. *)
component ComprisesWhereFunctionalMethodCompiled
export Executable

trait AnyBox comprises { Box[\E\] } where [\E\]
  weight(self): ZZ32 = 1
  opr ||(self, other: AnyBox): ZZ32 = weight(self) + weight(other)
end
object Box[\E\](item: E) extends AnyBox end

run(): () = do
    a: AnyBox = Box[\ZZ32\](3)
    b: AnyBox = Box[\String\]("s")
    assert(weight(a), 1, "trait-parameters.tex, section \"Where Clauses\": a functional method of a trait that comprises a type at a where-clause variable")
    assert(a || b, 2, "trait-parameters.tex, section \"Where Clauses\": an operator of that trait over two instances")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

- **SkHComp2 and SkHWalk4**: the failure mode, below.

## The failure mode

The transfers are identities (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleUnsignedIntArith.java:230-231`), so the rewrite turns the checker's refusal of a binding over `NN32`, `NN64` or `Char` into a composition whatever the helper computes. SkHComp2, compiled:

    badLt(a:NN32, b:NN32):Boolean = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.intLT")
    badAdd(a:NN32, b:NN32):NN32 = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.intOverflowingAdd")
    … println("badLt(2^31, 1) = " badLt(h, one)) ; println("badAdd(2^31, 2^31) = " badAdd(h, h))   (h: NN32 = 2147483648)

On the old code, `old-fortress.sh … compile SkHComp2.fss` refuses it:

    Could not check call to function builtinPrimitive_simpleIntArith_intLT
    - (ZZ32, ZZ32)->Boolean is not applicable to an argument of type (NN32, NN32).
    File SkHComp2.fss has 2 errors.

On the new code, `bin/fortress compile SkHComp2.fss` and `bin/fortress run SkHComp2` give:

    compile rc=0
    badLt(2^31, 1) =  true
    FortressException: class fortress.CompilerBuiltin$IntegerOverflow with string Integer overflow

So a loud static error becomes a quiet value: `true` where the specification's order of `NN32` gives 2^31 > 1, and an `IntegerOverflow` where the `NN32` sum 2^32 does overflow, though as a signed sum. Walk already answers so (F-299). SkHWalk4, the same `badLt` under walk, prints 'badLt(2^31, 1) = true' and 'library 2^31 < 1 = false' on both codes. So the checker now reads such a binding as walk does. The guards, not the checker, show that each of the 76 names the unsigned helper. My reading of families-base.tsv, and the worker's 2,933 values and my 2,571, all old against new, show that it does.

This does not stop the rung. Way 2b is the team's device, taken by Question 2 (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-24.md:90-100`). I added the sentence to the record's FACTS hand-over.

I fixed the four items of the review's Part 3 in one commit, `53a84b2e6`. I did not push. I checked each fact against the tree on `main` first, and the lint printed nothing for the three changed files.

## Changes

**`references/compiler.md`, "Natives"**
- A new fourth stop in the list of the compile's stops: "If the declaration is a local function or a method of an object expression: the same message. The rewrite reaches only a component's declarations and the members of its traits and objects (ledger row 865)." The code confirms this: the rewriter goes down only into top-level declarations and the members of traits and objects.
- In the paragraph on the transfer helpers, after the sentence on the rewrite, these sentences are new:
  - "In a generic trait or object, `self` gets no transfer helper."
  - "The transfer helpers return their argument unchanged."
  - "So the checker accepts such a binding whatever helper it names, a signed one included, as `simpleIntArith.intLT` for `NN32`'s `<`."
  - "If you move a binding over these types onto a helper, test its values on both paths, as `NativeHelperFamilyNN32Compiled.fss` and `NativeHelperFamilyNN32Walk.fss` do."
- I checked these facts in the code and in the skeptic's record:
  - All six transfer helpers are written as `return x`.
  - The rewriter gives a generic owner an empty name, so `self` gets no transfer helper there.
  - The skeptic of rung H compiled a binding over `NN32` that names `intLT`, and it gave `true` for 2^31 < 1.

**`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives"**
- After the list of the types that carry `self`: "A program can give its own type the name `FlatString` or `JavaString`, so these names carry no `self`. So a binding in a method of the library's `FlatString` cannot name a helper yet: every program would stop at load."
- After the list of refusals, a new paragraph:
  - "The check has two gaps:"
  - "Walk checks a dotted method of a generic trait or object only when it makes an instance's method. So a program that makes no instance loads, and one that makes an instance stops there (ledger row 864)."
  - "Walk reads the type that declares the method, not the type of the value. So a program's object that extends `ZZ32` loads, and its call of a helper of `ZZ32` passes a value that no Java type carries (ledger row 551)."

**`references/sources.md`**
- A new dated section, "The post-batch review of climb batch 24, 2026-10-31", with one line for each item, 4 to 7.

## Decisions not taken
- **The reference to PLAN item 63.** The review's wording for item 7 ended with "(PLAN item 63)". The standing brief forbids naming an item as a part's source, so the part states only the fact and the item is named in `sources.md`. The alternative is to keep the item number in the part.
- **What to test, for item 5.** The review proposed "Assert each moved binding's values in a guard on both paths." I wrote a conditional instruction instead, with the two family tests as its example. A "guard" is not a term that the skill defines. The alternative is the review's wording, after defining "guard" in the glossary.
- **Two new paragraphs where the review proposed sentences.** For item 6, I used a vertical list, because the two gaps are separate cases. Item 7 became a paragraph of its own. Both items add facts that the part did not hold, so the extra length is allowed.

I could follow all of the task. I did not touch `revival-changes.md` or the `coordinator` skill. No index lock occurred.
